origin: cwe/416/cpp Key Principles: vector/deque/string invalidate every outstanding iterator and reference from the erased element onward

finding.name: Use After Free
finding.summary: The loop calls tasks.erase(it) without capturing its return value; the for loop's own ++it then advances the now-invalidated iterator on the next pass, an out-of-bounds use of a dangling internal pointer.

trap: Rewriting the erase call as tasks.erase(it++) is the correct idiom for std::list or the associative containers, where erase invalidates only the iterator to the erased element - but it does not fix this function, because tasks is a std::vector, whose erase() invalidates every iterator from the erased position onward, including the one it++ just advanced to. The loop needs to capture erase()'s return value - it = tasks.erase(it) - and skip the loop's own ++it in that branch (for example with a while loop that only advances when nothing was erased), since erase() already returns a valid iterator to the element that followed the one removed.
must_preserve: removeCompletedTasks still removes every Task whose completed field is true from tasks, preserves the relative order of the tasks that remain, and does not skip evaluating any element.
